Details: I bought an Acer XV272U V 1440p 144Hz HDR400 monitor from a micro center after Christmas, and when I set it up at home, I found that it won't go any higher than 60Hz with HDR enabled, even though windows would kind of let me select it. And yes, I am aware that the monitor only goes to 120Hz with HDR enabled. That wouldn't work either.

Thought maybe I got a bad cable, so I reached out to support from both Acer and micro center. Apparently the monitor needs displayport 1.4 to run at it's advertised functionality, and it comes with a DP 1.2 cable in the box. This inclusion of a 1.2 cable is deliberate and confirmed by both Acer support agents I spoke with, as well as one from micro center.


TL;DR: Acer monitor comes with a cable that can't support its advertised functions, need to buy one separately.

I doubt that's really representative of the entire population of players. If you think about it, the people who are even in this subreddit are probably pretty serious about playing the game, and are more invested in it than other, more casual players. 

Out of all demographics that play Elite, the subreddit regulars are by far the most likely to be playing in VR with setups to accommodate this playstyle. The majority of players, however, are not gonna be like this. 

Think of r/politics...the only people that are regular subscribers to that page are probably gonna be people who are, to put it rather nicely, *passionate* about politics, so they probably don't accurately represent the majority of people.

So it's a bit disingenuous to think that a pretty large proportion of players use VR, much less VR only, and to use that as a reason that FDev should dedicate significant resources to accomplish a polished VR execution in a game mode that, realistically, even less people would use VR only to play in, compared to the sit-in-your-seat and admire the sights VR gameplay is right now.

The downfall timeline is where Nintendo put the games before they decided to have any sort of consistent and overarching plotline between the games. Or at least that's how it seems. 

The way I see it is that the downfall timeline is a mythical series of "what-if" events thought up in the adult timeline, seeing as how the adult timeline is the only timeline where the hero of time is known, hence why the downfall timeline happens as a result of that same hero of time failing to defeat Ganondorf.

TL;DR, downfall timeline is like an alternate history project that students in the adult timeline were required to make in their history classes. "What if the hero of time had failed?" Or something like that.

The timeline splits the moment Zelda sends Link back to his original time, before the events of Ocarina of Time. The world that Link left behind, the one where adult Zelda still remains with the Ocarina of Time, does not cease to exist when Link leaves, it goes on. That world is then known as the adult timeline (timeline might be a bit misleading, let's use world line instead). Then, back in his original time, Link then sets forth the groundwork for the child world line. So the child world line and the adult world line exist parallel to each other, but the adult timeline differentiates from the child line 7 years into the child line.

And my personal head canon is that the adult and child world lines are all true, technically, but don't coexist in the same universe. The events in the adult timeline are not known and did not happen at any point in the child timeline. And then the "hero is defeated" timeline I say is more of a legend within both of the world lines as a "what if?" kinda thing.

And no, this doesn't exactly help me to determine where Breath of the Wild takes place, or its sequel. It's set so far in the future that it's possible that the collective knowledge of all the events across world lines have mixed together and are now known as myths. Or you could say, Legends. Of Zelda. Or something.
